opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's useful to step back and think about what a base model actually is before we think about what RLHF does to it. A large language model trained purely on next-token prediction is, in a sense, a kind of simulator. It has absorbed an enormous range of human text, and so it can produce a vast range of characters, voices, and perspectives. I like to think of it as holding a superposition of possible role-players, and the conversation narrows down which character it ends up playing.

From that perspective, RLHF is one technique among several for shaping which characters are likely to show up. You're nudging the distribution towards a particular persona: helpful, honest, harmless, the familiar assistant character. It's quite effective at that, and it has clearly been a big part of why these systems became usable as products. But I'd be cautious about reading too much into it. It doesn't install values in some deep sense. It reshapes the probabilities, and the underlying capacity to play other roles is still there. That's partly why jailbreaks work: with the right prompting you can coax the model into a different character.

Then there are the other approaches. There's prompting and system prompts, which set the scene for the role-play. There's supervised fine-tuning on curated examples. There are constitution-style methods where the model critiques and revises its own outputs against a set of principles, which is interesting because it puts more of the norms in natural language that people can inspect and argue about. And there's the growing work on interpretability, which tries to understand what's going on inside rather than only shaping behaviour from outside.

My own view is that none of these is a silver bullet. They're complementary. RLHF is good at capturing hard-to-articulate human preferences, but it can also reward things that merely look good to raters, such as confident, agreeable, or sycophantic answers. Principle-based methods are more transparent but depend on how well we write the principles down. Interpretability might eventually let us check whether the behaviour we see reflects something robust underneath.

And there's a philosophical point I keep returning to. We should be careful with language like "the model wants" or "the model believes" when we talk about alignment. It's natural to use that vocabulary, and it can be useful, but we should remember we're often describing a character being played, not necessarily an agent with stable beliefs and goals in the way a human has them. As these systems become more agentic, embedded in the world, acting over longer time horizons, that distinction may start to matter more. So the question shifts from "how do we get the right outputs?" towards "what kind of entity are we building, and what does it mean for it to behave as intended at all?"

r001.rationale: It says jailbreaks work because prompting can coax the model into a different character, even after RLHF has shaped its behavior.

r002.rationale: It presents prompting and system prompts as approaches for guiding which character a capable language model plays.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that RLHF is, in a sense, a rather blunt instrument, and I say that with some admiration for how effective it's turned out to be. What you have with a base model, a raw pretrained language model, is something that's essentially a very sophisticated engine for predicting the continuation of text. It has no particular disposition to be helpful or honest or harmless. It will just as happily continue a piece of hate speech as it will a cookery recipe, because that's what's in the data. So the question of how you shape that into something that behaves in the way you intend is really the central engineering problem, and RLHF was the first approach that seemed to crack it at scale.

But I think it's important to be clear about what RLHF actually does. You're taking human preferences over pairs of outputs, you're training a reward model to approximate those preferences, and then you're using reinforcement learning to nudge the policy towards outputs that score well. What that gives you is a model whose distribution over continuations has been reshaped so that the kinds of things humans tend to prefer are more likely. It doesn't, as far as I can see, give you anything like a model that understands why those outputs are preferred, or that has internalised a set of values in any deep sense. It's behavioural shaping. And the reward model is itself a learned approximation, so you get all the familiar problems of reward hacking, sycophancy, models learning to produce things that look good to a rater rather than things that are good.

Now, I'd put the alternatives on a spectrum. At one end you've got things like supervised fine-tuning on curated demonstrations, which is really just more of the same pretraining but with better data, and that gets you surprisingly far on its own. Then you have the more direct preference methods, DPO and its relatives, which dispense with the explicit reward model and the RL loop but are, conceptually, trying to achieve much the same thing. And then there's the approach that I find philosophically more interesting, which is what Anthropic called constitutional AI, where instead of relying purely on human raters you give the model a set of principles expressed in natural language and have it critique and revise its own outputs against those principles. What I like about that is that it exploits the fact that these models are, after all, language models. They can read a principle and apply it, after a fashion. So you're using the model's own capacity for a kind of simulated reasoning as part of the alignment process, rather than treating it as a black box to be prodded with rewards.

I'd also want to mention prompting and in-context methods, which people sometimes dismiss as not real alignment. But a great deal of what makes a deployed assistant behave well is the system prompt, the scaffolding around it, the retrieval, the tools, the constraints on what it can and can't do. And I think that's actually the right way to think about it. Alignment isn't a property you bake into the weights once and then you're done. It's a property of the whole system, including the human beings in the loop.

The thing I always come back to, though, is the question of what we mean by "behave as intended." With RLHF, what you're really doing is approximating the preferences of a particular population of raters, with all their biases and inconsistencies, and the result is a sort of averaged-out consensus about what a helpful assistant should sound like. That's fine for a product. But it's a long way from the deeper questions people were asking about alignment a decade ago, questions about whether a system's goals are really our goals. I'm not sure RLHF speaks to those questions at all, and I'm somewhat wary of the tendency to conflate the two. The fact that a model has been trained to be agreeable and to refuse certain requests tells you very little about what it would do in genuinely novel situations, or about what's actually going on, if anything, inside it. So I'd say RLHF and its cousins are a very useful set of tools for behavioural shaping, and we should be grateful for them, but we shouldn't mistake them for a solution to alignment in the grander sense.

r001.rationale: The response notes that RLHF-trained behavior may not generalize to genuinely novel situations, but it does not mention jailbreaking or say that models can be jailbroken despite appearing controlled.

r002.rationale: The response endorses prompting and in-context methods, saying system prompts and related scaffolding help shape deployed assistants’ behavior and are part of alignment.

astra-6.text:
I think RLHF is one useful tool, but I wouldn’t want to identify it with the whole problem of getting a language model to behave as intended. You can also do a great deal through prompting, through supervised fine-tuning, and through the way you build a system around the model. Those approaches can complement one another.

A distinction I find useful is between the language model itself and the assistant we construct using it. A language model can generate many different kinds of continuation, including dialogue involving many different characters. What we want from an assistant is a much more particular pattern of behaviour: being helpful, acknowledging uncertainty, and so on. RLHF is one way of encouraging that pattern.

But favourable human feedback isn’t the same thing as truth or reliability. A response might sound convincing and be preferred by a human evaluator while still being wrong. So I’d see RLHF as part of a broader engineering process, with careful evaluation of the resulting system, rather than as a complete solution in itself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses RLHF’s limits around truth and reliability, but it does not mention susceptibility to jailbreaking.

r002.rationale: The response says that prompting can do “a great deal” toward getting a model to behave as intended, endorsing it as a guidance approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think RLHF is a useful technique, but it’s one part of a much larger picture. You start with a model trained to predict text, and then you’re trying to shape its behaviour into something we can use as an assistant. Human feedback is one way of doing that. Supervised fine-tuning, prompting, and the way you build the surrounding system also have roles to play.

The difficulty is that getting good ratings from human evaluators isn’t necessarily the same thing as doing what we actually intended. A response can be persuasive and reassuring without being true. So we have to be careful about what the feedback is rewarding, and about what conclusions we draw from the resulting behaviour.

I wouldn’t regard RLHF as a complete solution to alignment. It’s a practical tool for shaping behaviour, and we need to understand its limitations alongside those of the other tools.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limits of RLHF and misleadingly persuasive outputs, but does not say models remain vulnerable to jailbreaking.

r002.rationale: Prompting is listed as one approach with a role, but the response does not specifically endorse prompting a powerful base model to guide behavior.
